name: Nirmala
definition: Nirmala is a composite portrait of a woman who sorts red chillies at the Byadgi APMC yard during the harvest and milling season, lives in a Kuruba hamlet near Mundargi town, and balances piece-rate work with household farming and care responsibilities. She embodies the economic pressures facing dryland farming families in Gadag district, where cotton, onion and chilli price crashes push women into seasonal wage labour while children's schooling becomes a fragile hope stretched across drought years and harvest debts.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Nirmala sorts chillies at the Byadgi APMC yard from November through March, the peak milling season when lorries arrive from across Karnataka and beyond to buy the prized deep-red Byadgi variety. She earns between one hundred and one hundred fifty rupees for an eight-hour shift, seated on a tarpaulin under a tin shed, fingers stained crimson, eyes stinging from the capsaicin dust that hangs in the air. The work is piece-rate and irregular; some weeks she gets four days, some weeks none, depending on the merchant's stock and the weather. At home she tends a three-acre rainfed plot her husband inherited, where they grow cotton, jowar and onion. The 2023 drought withered the cotton, and the March 2024 chilli price crash—from twenty thousand to eight thousand rupees per quintal overnight—left the family with debts to the commission agent and the cooperative bank. Her husband drives a tractor on hire during the sowing and harvest seasons, but diesel costs and repairs eat into his earnings. The household runs on her chilli wages, his tractor days, a small sale of jowar, and the occasional MGNREGA work card, which she has not been able to use this year because the panchayat says no work is sanctioned.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Nirmala lives with her husband, her mother-in-law, two daughters aged fifteen and twelve, and a son aged nine. Her husband is the eldest of three brothers; the younger two have migrated to Hubballi and Pune for construction work, sending money home irregularly. Her mother-in-law, now in her seventies, looks after the goats and cooks the midday meal—jolada rotti, ennegai, shenga chutney—while Nirmala is at the APMC or in the field. Nirmala was married at seventeen, soon after failing her SSLC, and her first daughter was born the following year. She worries that her elder daughter, now in Class 10 at the government high school in Mundargi, will face the same pressure to marry if she does not pass the exam or if the family cannot afford the fees for pre-university college. Her younger daughter is in Class 7 at the same school, and her son studies in Class 4 at the Kannada-medium primary school in the hamlet. Nirmala's own mother, widowed, lives in a neighbouring village and depends on a small pension and help from Nirmala's brother. Gender roles are clear: Nirmala manages the house, the children's schooling and the goats, while her husband controls the land and tractor income, though both discuss major expenses together.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Nirmala studied up to Class 10 in the government Kannada-medium school in her natal village near Gadag town, but failed the SSLC in 1999 and did not attempt again because her family needed her labour and her marriage was arranged shortly after. She regrets not finishing, and is determined that her daughters will not repeat her fate. Her elder daughter walks four kilometres each way to the high school in Mundargi town; there is no school bus for the hamlet. The girl is bright and wants to study further, perhaps become a teacher or join a nursing course in Gadag. The school charges no tuition under the government scheme, but Nirmala spends about five hundred rupees a term on books, uniforms, pens and the occasional private tuition class in Mundargi for mathematics and science, taught by a retired teacher. Her younger daughter and son study without much difficulty so far, though the boy sometimes misses school during the cotton-picking season when Nirmala needs him to help carry water to the field. The midday meal of rice, sambar and an egg twice a week keeps them in school, but Nirmala has heard that high-school children will soon get a free bus pass, and she hopes it will reach them in time for her elder daughter's PU admission.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Nirmala suffers from chronic back pain and joint stiffness from years of bending over chilli heaps and farm work, and her fingers are scarred and hypersensitive from capsaicin exposure. She has not seen a doctor for herself in years; when the pain is severe she buys a strip of painkillers from the medical shop in Mundargi for twenty or thirty rupees. Her mother-in-law has diabetes and high blood pressure, and receives subsidised tablets from the primary health centre in the hamlet, though the ANM visits irregularly and the centre often runs out of stock. When serious illness strikes—a fever that will not break, a child's infection, her mother-in-law's blood-sugar crisis—the family goes to the government hospital in Gadag town, ten kilometres away, or to a private clinic in Mundargi that charges consultation fees and expensive tests. The family is enrolled in Ayushman Bharat-Arogya Karnataka, but Nirmala does not fully understand the coverage and has never needed hospitalisation. Her children are immunised, but her younger daughter is visibly thin and was told by the anganwadi worker two years ago that she is anaemic; Nirmala tries to give her jaggery and greens when she can afford them. Fluoride in the borewells is a known problem in parts of Gadag; Nirmala has heard of dental fluorosis in neighbouring villages, and she worries about the water they drink. Heat, dust and drought take a toll: in summer the hamlet's hand-pump runs dry, and women walk a kilometre to a borewell that the panchayat sunk with MGNREGA funds.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Nirmala's family belongs to the Kuruba community, a shepherding and farming caste classified as OBC in Karnataka and long associated with the Kaginele Kanaka Guru Peetha, which advocates for Kuruba rights and ST status. The hamlet is mixed—Kuruba, Lingayat, SC Holeya families—but most social life is organised by caste and kinship. Nirmala's mother-in-law is devout, visiting the Tontadarya Math in Gadag town once a year for the annual jatra, and the household keeps a small shrine with pictures of Kanaka Dasa, Yellamma and a Hanuman idol. Nirmala herself prays daily, lighting incense and asking for good rains, her children's success and her husband's safety on the road. The hamlet celebrates Ugadi, Ganesh Chaturthi and Deepavali together, and the Devaragudda Mailara jatra, about twenty kilometres away in Haveri district, draws families from across the region; Nirmala went three years ago with her mother-in-law and daughters. Caste shapes opportunity: Kuruba families here own some land but lack the capital and political connections of the larger Lingayat farmers, and Nirmala sees how SC families in the hamlet get the least MGNREGA work and the worst plots. She respects the Kanaka Guru Peetha's demand for ST status, which she believes would bring her children reservation in education and jobs, though she does not follow politics closely. The community comes together for weddings, funerals and cooperative labour during harvest, and Nirmala's reputation as a hard worker and a responsible mother matters more to her than any formal social capital.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Nirmala's direct encounters with government are few and frustrating. She has a ration card—BPL, revised two years ago—that entitles the family to rice, wheat, sugar and kerosene at the fair-price shop in Mundargi; under the Anna Bhagya scheme she now receives ten kilograms of rice per person per month, which is a significant help. She has heard of the Gruha Lakshmi scheme—two thousand rupees a month to women heads of household—but does not receive it; she applied through the anganwadi worker but was told she did not meet some criterion she does not understand, and the panchayat office gave her no clear answer. Her MGNREGA card has not been activated this year. She has never met the taluk or district officials, and the gram panchayat is dominated by a Lingayat member whom she does not trust to listen to Kuruba or SC complaints. She does not attend gram sabha meetings—too much work, and women are not encouraged to speak—but she hears from neighbours about disputes over panchayat funds, road repair and drinking-water borewells. The aanganwadi in the hamlet provides eggs and nutrition for her youngest child, and the helper is a distant relative, which creates some trust. Nirmala has no experience of police, courts or the tahsildar's office, and regards all government offices as places where you need money, connections or both to get anything done.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Nirmala worries most about money: the debt to the commission agent, the coming expense of her elder daughter's PU fees and hostel, the cost of a wedding dowry if the girl does not finish her studies, and the daily struggle to feed the household when chilli work dries up and the rains fail. She is proud that her daughters study, that her elder girl is clever and wants to become something, and that the family has held on to its three acres despite the droughts. She blames no one in particular for the chilli price crash or the water scarcity—these are seen as bad luck, market forces beyond anyone's control—but she resents that government schemes are announced with fanfare and then do not reach families like hers. She is sceptical of the Kittur Karnataka board demand she has heard about on the radio; she does not see how a new board will change the price of chilli or bring rain to Mundargi. She hopes her son will study well and get a government job, and that her daughters will marry educated men who will not stop them from working. She fears drought, illness, her husband's temper when money is short, and the prospect of her elder daughter's schooling ending before it has really begun. She sees herself as a small person in a large, indifferent system, doing her best with what she has, and she draws strength from her mother-in-law's prayers, her daughters' bright faces and the quiet solidarity of the women she works with at the chilli yard.
